summary: The Gemara clarifies that the altar’s purity means its exposed top, resolves the order and placement of blood applications, determines that the tamid-olah receives the chatat-style procedure, and contrasts the Tamid mishna’s placement of the Chamber of the Lambs in the northwest corner of the Temple courtyard, among four chambers that included the Beit HaMoked, with the Middot mishna’s placement of it in the southwest corner of the Beit HaMoked structure itself.

display.title: Tohoro resolved: 'purity' means the altar's bare top surface
display.oneLine: Rabba bar Sheila identifies the altar's 'tohoro' as its exposed top surface.
display.whats: Rabba bar Sheila resolves the final question from 15a about 'tohoro': what does 'the purity of the altar' mean? He answers that it means the top surface of the altar itself. The verse 'like the very sky for purity' supplies the usage of the word, and the altar's top is where the incense ashes are cleared away and the pure gold becomes visible.
display.hint: How does the verse's use of 'purity' help identify the altar's cleared top, where its pure gold is visible?

learning.learnerQuestion: What part of the altar does the term 'tohoro,' its purity, refer to?
learning.coreTension: 'Tohoro' (purity) is an abstract word, but the sugya needs it to identify a concrete physical location on the altar where blood is sprinkled.
learning.coreMove: Rabba bar Sheila identifies 'tohoro' as the altar's top surface by citing the verse 'like the very sky for purity'; after the incense ashes are cleared from that surface, the pure gold is visible.
learning.learningBlocker: It is tempting to hear 'purity' and think of a specially sanctified zone rather than a plain physical surface. The verse proof shows the term is doing ordinary descriptive work: the top is 'pure' simply because it is the cleared, exposed face of the altar.

takeaway.text: An ambiguous term in a halakhic ruling can be fixed to a precise physical referent by citing a verse that uses the same term in an unambiguous descriptive sense elsewhere.

learning.ahaMoment: The word 'purity' (tohoro) is being used architecturally - the 'pure part' of the altar is its top, the part exposed and cleared of incense ash.
learning.memoryAnchor: Tohoro = the altar top: incense ashes cleared away, pure gold visible. 'Like the very sky for purity' supplies the word's usage.

argumentFlow.label: Rabba bar Sheila: tohoro = altar top
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabba bar Sheila
argumentFlow.text: Tohoro refers to the top surface of the altar itself. The verse 'like the very sky for purity' supplies the usage of the term; after the incense ashes are cleared from the altar's top, its pure gold is visible.

misconceptions.misconception: A natural but incorrect assumption is that 'tohoro' names a special, separately sanctified section of the altar.
misconceptions.correction: It simply means the altar's top surface, the part exposed and cleared, not a distinct sanctified zone.

visualizableElements.item: Diagram of the altar's top surface (tohoro), showing the incense ashes cleared away and the pure gold visible.

quizSeeds.question: What does 'tohoro shel mizbeach' mean and how does Rabba bar Sheila prove it?
quizSeeds.answer: It means the top surface of the altar. Rabba bar Sheila cites 'like the very sky for purity' for the usage of the term; the altar's top is where the incense ashes are cleared away and the pure gold becomes visible.

sugyot.finalRuling: Rabba bar Sheila establishes from the verse that tohoro means the altar's bare top surface.

glossary.en: For purity - the word quoted from Exodus 24:10 to establish the usage of tohoro for the altar's cleared top, where its pure gold is visible.

prerequisiteKnowledge: The altar's top is exposed after the incense ashes are cleared.

display.title: Three loose ends in R. Shimon's blood choreography, each tied off
display.oneLine: Why olah comes before chatat, why the northeast-southwest pair of corners is used rather than the southeast-northwest pair, and why the northeast corner comes first are each resolved with a specific answer.
display.whats: Three follow-up questions about R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah's blood-sprinkling procedure are resolved. First: why perform the olah procedure before the chatat procedure? Second: why use the northeast and southwest corners rather than the southeast and northwest corners? Third: why begin at the northeast corner rather than the southwest corner?
display.hint: Why does olah come first, why is its blood applied at the northeastern corner, and why is that corner encountered first?

learning.learnerQuestion: R. Shimon's dual olah-and-chatat blood rite raises three practical questions: why does the olah procedure come first, why are the northeast and southwest corners used instead of the southeast and northwest corners, and why does the northeast corner come first?
learning.coreTension: Each question exposes a place where the abstract dual-requirement ruling has to meet a concrete physical constraint of the altar (sequence, foundation structure, walking direction), and it is not obvious in advance that the ruling survives contact with those constraints.
learning.coreMove: Each question is resolved by a specific fact: the tamid is an olah, the southeastern corner lacks the yesod required for olah blood so the northeastern corner is used instead, and the rule of rightward turns makes the priest encounter the northeastern corner first.
learning.learningBlocker: It is easy to expect one unifying explanation for all three difficulties. Instead each is resolved independently, by a different specific principle, showing that a complex ritual choreography can rest on several narrow technical facts rather than one grand rule.

takeaway.text: A ritual procedure built from two overlapping sacrificial categories can be fully specified, sequence, exceptions, and direction of movement, once each point of friction is matched to its own governing principle rather than forced under a single explanation.

learning.ahaMoment: Each question has a precise technical answer - the sugya is showing how halakhic principles interact when a single act must satisfy two different sacrificial categories.
learning.memoryAnchor: Three questions, three answers: (1) olah first because the tamid is an olah, (2) southeast lacks a yesod, so use northeast, (3) turn right and encounter northeast first.

argumentFlow.label: Why olah before chatat in the corner sequence?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: R. Shimon prescribes sprinkling in the olah manner first and then in the chatat manner. Why does the olah procedure take priority?

sourceRefs.note: First question: why olah before chatat

argumentFlow.label: Tamid IS an olah - so olah comes first
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The tamid itself is an olah. The olah identity precedes the chatat identity in this sacrifice, so olah-applications come first.

sourceRefs.note: Resolution: tamid is inherently an olah

argumentFlow.label: Why northeast and southwest rather than southeast and northwest?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Why is the blood applied at the northeastern and southwestern corners rather than the southeastern and northwestern corners?

sourceRefs.note: Second question about the choice of corners

argumentFlow.label: The southeast lacks a yesod, so the northeast is used
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Olah blood requires a yesod below its application point. The southeastern corner lacks a yesod, so the blood is applied at the northeastern corner instead, which does have one.

argumentFlow.label: Why is the northeastern corner reached before the southwestern corner?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Why is blood applied first at the northeastern corner rather than at the southwestern corner?

sourceRefs.note: Third question about direction of approach

argumentFlow.label: All altar turns go right, so northeast is encountered first
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: All turns made at the altar go only to the right, toward the east, so the priest encounters the northeastern corner first while circling the altar.

sourceRefs.note: Resolution by the rule of rightward turns

misconceptions.misconception: R. Shimon applies olah-style blood at the same corner regardless of yesod availability.
misconceptions.correction: The southeastern corner lacks a yesod, so R. Shimon's olah-blood application moves to the northeastern corner, which does have one.

visualizableElements.item: Altar diagram showing the southeastern corner without a yesod and the blood applications at the northeastern and southwestern corners
Three-panel sequence: (1) olah first because the tamid is an olah; (2) southeast lacks a yesod, so northeast is used; (3) rightward movement encounters northeast first

quizSeeds.question: Why does R. Shimon ish HaMitzpah prescribe olah-style sprinkling before chatat-style sprinkling?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the tamid is inherently an olah - its primary identity is as a burnt offering, so the olah application has priority.

sourceRefs.note: Resolution: tamid is inherently an olah

quizSeeds.question: How is the northeast corner problem resolved in R. Shimon's blood rite?
quizSeeds.answer: The southeastern corner has no yesod, so the olah blood application, which requires a yesod, is placed at the northeastern corner instead.

quizSeeds.question: Why is blood applied at the northeastern corner before the southwestern corner?
quizSeeds.answer: All turns made at the altar go only to the right, toward the east, so the priest encounters the northeastern corner first while circling the altar.

sourceRefs.note: Resolution by the rule of rightward turns

sugyot.finalRuling: The three specific follow-up questions about R. Shimon’s corner sequence are resolved within this passage: the tamid is an olah, the southeastern corner lacks a yesod, and rightward movement reaches the northeastern corner first.

glossary.en: The altar's foundation ledge. In the olah discussion, its absence at the southeast corner requires the blood application at the northeast corner instead.

prerequisiteKnowledge: Olah blood applications require a yesod below
The southeastern corner of the altar lacks a yesod

display.title: Which way does the equation run? Reading 'chatat upon olah'
display.oneLine: The Gemara proves that the tamid-olah receives the chatat-style blood procedure, rather than the New Moon chatat receiving the olah procedure.
display.whats: Does the Torah apply the chatat procedure to the tamid-olah, or apply the olah procedure to the New Moon chatat? The verse about offering the chatat in addition to the tamid-olah settles which offering receives the other's procedure.
display.hint: Which offering does the verse prove receives the other offering's blood procedure?

learning.learnerQuestion: Does the tamid-olah receive the chatat procedure, or does the New Moon chatat receive the olah procedure?
learning.coreTension: The two offerings and two blood procedures can be paired in opposite ways: chatat procedure on the tamid-olah, or olah procedure on the New Moon chatat.
learning.coreMove: The verse stating that the chatat is offered in addition to the tamid-olah establishes that the chatat matter is cast onto the olah: the tamid receives the chatat-style blood procedure.
learning.learningBlocker: The difficulty is keeping straight which offering receives the other offering's blood procedure; the verse identifies the tamid-olah as the offering modified by the chatat procedure.

takeaway.text: When two offerings and their procedures are linked, the verse can determine which offering receives the other's procedure; here the tamid-olah receives the chatat-style application.

learning.ahaMoment: The proof identifies not merely a procedure but its recipient: the chatat procedure is applied to the tamid-olah.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two possibilities: chatat procedure on tamid-olah, or olah procedure on New Moon chatat. The verse chooses the tamid-olah.

argumentFlow.label: Which offering receives the other's procedure?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Does the Torah require chatat-style blood application on the tamid-olah, or olah-style blood application on the New Moon chatat? The verse proves that the chatat procedure is applied to the tamid-olah.

sourceRefs.note: Question about which offering’s procedure is applied to the other

misconceptions.misconception: The alternative is whether chatat blood is physically poured onto the olah animal.
misconceptions.correction: The actual alternatives are chatat procedure on the tamid-olah or olah procedure on the New Moon chatat; the verse proves the first.

visualizableElements.item: Two offerings and two possible procedure pairings: chatat procedure on the tamid-olah versus olah procedure on the New Moon chatat

quizSeeds.question: Which offering receives the other offering's blood procedure?
quizSeeds.answer: The alternatives are chatat procedure on the tamid-olah or olah procedure on the New Moon chatat. The verse proves that the tamid-olah receives the chatat-style procedure.

sourceRefs.note: Directional question about the verse equation

sugyot.finalRuling: The tamid-olah receives the chatat-style blood application, not the reverse.

display.title: Same Temple, two floor plans: the Chamber of the Lambs contradiction opens 16a
display.oneLine: Tractate Tamid and Tractate Middot place the Chamber of the Lambs in different corners of the Beit HaMoked, leaving a contradiction unresolved here.
display.whats: The mishna from Tractate Tamid places the Chamber of the Lambs in one corner, while Tractate Middot's mishna places it in a different corner, with the contradiction continuing on the next page.
display.hint: How can Tractate Tamid and Tractate Middot place the Chamber of the Lambs in different corners?

learning.learnerQuestion: Tamid and Middot both describe the four-chamber Beit HaMoked, but they put the Chamber of the Lambs in different corners. How can two descriptions of the same physical room disagree?
learning.coreTension: The mishna from Tractate Tamid locates the Chamber of the Lambs in one corner of the Beit HaMoked, while Tractate Middot's description places it in a different corner.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara raises the contradiction between the Tamid mishna, which places the Chamber of the Lambs in the northwest, and the Middot mishna, which places it in the southwest, and leaves the contradiction unresolved here.
learning.learningBlocker: It is easy to expect an outright resolution, but this amud only presents the two conflicting locations and leaves the contradiction open.

takeaway.text: The Chamber of the Lambs is placed in different corners by Tamid and Middot. This sugya raises the contradiction without resolving which location is correct; the discussion continues on the next daf.

learning.ahaMoment: The contradiction between Tamid’s and Middot’s placements of the Chamber of the Lambs is raised here and left open for the next amud to resolve.
learning.memoryAnchor: Chamber of the Lambs: two locations, two tractates, one Temple. The contradiction launches the 16a debate.

argumentFlow.label: Tamid: Chamber of Lambs in one location
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishna
argumentFlow.text: A mishna from Tractate Tamid, cited here in the Gemara of Yoma, places the Chamber of the Lambs in one corner.

argumentFlow.label: Middot places it in a different corner
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Tractate Middot's description of the four Beit HaMoked chambers places the Chamber of the Lambs in a different corner, creating a direct contradiction.

argumentFlow.label: The two mishnayot contradict one another
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Tamid mishna places the Chamber of the Lambs in the northwest, while Middot places it in the southwest. The contradiction is presented here; its resolution is taken up on the next daf.

sourceRefs.note: Middot's southwest placement creates the contradiction

misconceptions.misconception: Tractates always agree on Temple topography since they describe the same physical structure.
misconceptions.correction: Different tractates may reflect different authorities with different spatial perspectives, producing genuine contradictions like the Chamber of the Lambs location.

quizSeeds.answer: Both tractates describe the four-chamber Beit HaMoked, but they place the Chamber of the Lambs in different corners. The contradiction is raised here and continues on the next page.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Against its own body of the altar' - on its roof; and what is the meaning of the term 'tohoro' (its purity)? Because it purifies and clears away
the ash of the incense that was burned on it in the morning, sweeping it aside, and he sprinkles on the spot
that has been uncovered, as it is written, 'and like the essence of the heavens for purity (latohar)' - like 'letaher.' 'A burnt-offering requires
a base' - meaning its blood must be placed where there is a base beneath it, for so
we say in Zevachim (51a): 'do not place blood upon the base
of the altar; for the slaughtered blood of a burnt-offering there must be
a base beneath it.' 'The southeastern
corner had no base' - as we say
in tractate Middot (3:1): the base
ran along the whole north, and
along the whole west, extending on the east one cubit
at the point the north side ended toward the east, and on the south
one cubit at the point the west side ended toward the south -
from which it follows that there was no base at the southeastern corner
and we say in Zevachim (53b): because
the cubit-wide base of the whole east
and of the whole south fell within Binyamin's portion,
as we translate: 'in his inheritance was built
the altar' (Genesis 49) - therefore there was no
base for it. 'Since the master said, etc.' -
this is from Rami bar Yechezkel's mishna,
later (58b). 'They may only be by way of
the right, toward the east' - here 'toward the east' does not apply,
but in Zevachim it applies, to teach it, since it deals
there with placing the altar's ramp to the south
and derives it from 'and its steps facing east' -
read: place its steps to the south, so that the beginning of
its turns faces east when one turns to the right,
since all turns are by way of the right - for Rami
bar Yechezkel taught: 'standing upon twelve
oxen,' etc.; and because of that version, he uses
'toward the east' everywhere, though properly one could only say
'by way of the right' and nothing more. 'In the first corner
he encountered' - when he goes up the ramp and turns
to the right, he first encounters the southeastern corner
first, and there it is impossible to place blood, because
it has no base; so he circles around and comes to the northeastern
corner and places it there. And although the placing of blood is not
done via the ramp, since he stands on the floor
with the vessel in hand and casts it from a distance, as it is written,
'and he shall cast it' - since he places it below the scarlet thread -
nevertheless, since for a sin-offering, whose blood is placed on the upper part of the corner, he must go up
the ramp by way of the south and turn to the east, so too for all blood placements, even though he places them
below, he begins circling from the south, which is the face of the altar, like the entrance
of the Sanctuary, and turns right from there. 'Perhaps regarding a sin-offering' - of the New Moon,
of which the Merciful One said, perform on it the act of a burnt-offering. 'That cannot enter your mind, for it is written' - 'as a sin-offering
in addition to a burnt-offering.' 'We learned there' - in tractate Tamid, though it is not truly fitting to place it in the Gemara
of the order of the day, except that it deals above with a similar kind of switch: which tanna
taught the order of the day? It is Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpah; we do not derive this from his having explicitly said so,
but rather because we heard that he disputes the order of the daily-offering; they establish the unattributed teaching
that disputes the daily-offering as following his view, and since no such school of thought is otherwise found in the Gemara, they fix
this one too alongside it, since it can likewise be established on that same view. 'The appointed one' - that is the deputy High Priest
'And they brought, etc.' - the daily offering. 'From the chamber of the lambs' - for the lambs were kept there,
examined, as we learned (Arachin 13a): 'they use no fewer than six examined lambs
in the chamber of the lambs.' 'But was it not' - like saying 'but it was in such-and-such a place.' 'At the corner
northwestern' - of the chamber of the hearth, which was a large hall, where they would light
great bonfires, to warm the priests who walked barefoot on the pavement
of the courtyard, which was of marble; and at its corners were chambers, opening like small rooms

opening onto the hall, as is taught further; and there were four chambers there, at the four corners - one being the chamber of the lambs, and so on. 'The chamber of the seals' - where they would place
the seals of one who purchases flour-offerings and libations from the Temple treasury for money, as we learned in tractate Shekalim (7b): 'there were four seals in the Temple, and on them was written
calf, goat, male, sinner' - these being tokens for a sheep, a ram, a bull, and the three animals of a leper; whoever requests libations comes to the one appointed over the seals
and gives him money according to the libations he needs, and receives from him a seal for those libations; then he comes to the one appointed over the libations and shows him the seal,

and receives the libations from him, and so on, as is explained there. 'The chamber of the hearth' - a small chamber called the chamber of the hearth, opening into the great chamber of the hearth. 'Where they make in it'

the showbread' - the house of Garmu made the preparation of the showbread there. 'To the chamber of the hearth' - opening onto it. 'Two in sanctified ground and two outside it' - of the chamber of the hearth,

part of it was built within the sanctified courtyard, and part of it outside. 'And the tops of the partitions' - pieces of wood marking, as a sign, the point that divides sanctified from non-sanctified
'Which had been profaned' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (explaining that the kings of the idolatrous nations burned incense there for idol worship) continues on 16a.
